items.title: Fix temporaries leaking when a VM interrupt throws at the op that fre…
items.body:
The VM checks for interrupts after setting `opline` to the next op, such as a jump target (and, in the CALL VM, the op after a call to a user function); the JIT checks at loop headers and in side-exit stubs. If the interrupt function throws (async pcntl signal handler, Excimer timeout, ...), the exception is attributed to that op, which has not run. Live ranges end at the op that consumes a var, so `ZEND_HANDLE_EXCEPTION` does not free vars that this op was about to consume:

```php
function gen() { yield 1; release(); } // interrupt pending as release() returns
foreach (gen() as $v) {}               // FE_FETCH jumps to FE_FREE: generator leaks
```

The same happens with `switch` on a string, and with ternary/`match` results assigned after the jump.

The interrupt helpers already undefine the result of the interrupted op. This PR moves that to `zend_cleanup_interrupted_op()`, which also frees vars whose live range ends at the interrupted op, and the operand defined by the op just before it (which has no live range). Interrupt timing is unchanged.

Tests use `zend_test.observer.set_vm_interrupt_on_end` (also added by the fix for GH-24480), which makes an interrupt pending and throwing as an observed function returns.

Tested on debug builds of the hybrid and CALL VMs, without opcache and with opcache with JIT off, function JIT and tracing JIT.

items.title: php8.6: Fix set visibility bypass through a primed ZEND_ASSIGN_OBJ cache slot
Fix GH-24438: Preserve indirect types in JIT side traces
items.body:
Fixes #24438

the tracing jit can enter a side trace at `SEND_FUNC_ARG` after a `FETCH_DIM_FUNC_ARG` has already executed in the parent trace.

when regular ssa information isn't available, `zend_jit_trace_build_tssa()` initializes live-in temporaries with a fallback type mask that doesn't include `MAY_BE_INDIRECT`. this can leave an indirect operand without the corresponding type information.

`zend_jit_send_ref()` relies on that bit to emit the conditional indirect dereference. without it, the jit can handle the temporary incorrectly when a dynamic call switches between by-value and by-reference arguments.

the fix adds `MAY_BE_INDIRECT` to the temporary fallback mask. it also adds a phpt regression test that alternates between by-value and by-reference calls and verifies that the correct array elements are updated.

i tested the change on php 8.5.13-dev using linux x86_64 debug nts builds from the same source revision. the original implementation fails the regression test with an assertion in `zval_get_long_func()`, while the patched version passes with the expected values.

the full `ext/opcache/tests/jit/` suite completed with 515 passes, no failures and 10 skips due to missing extensions or platform requirements.

i also verified that the original reproducer produces the same warnings as the interpreter after the fix. additional checks involving existing references, array aliasing and copy-on-write behavior matched interpreter results.

the original issue reproduces on php 8.4.28-dev as well. the patch was developed and validated on php 8.5; php 8.4 patch validation is not yet included in these results.

release, zts and other architectures haven't been tested locally.

items.title: OPcache: file cache loses attributes on constants on 32-bit builds
items.body:
### Description

I prepared this report with an LLM. I ran the reproduction and the controls myself, on the Docker images named below.

The following code:

`foo.php`:
```php
<?php

#[Deprecated(message: 'bar')]
const FOO = 1;
```

`test.php`:
```php
<?php

require __DIR__ . '/foo.php';

var_dump((new ReflectionConstant('FOO'))->getAttributes()[0]->getArguments());
```

Run two times on a 32-bit build:
```
php -d opcache.enable_cli=1 -d opcache.file_cache=/tmp/opcache -d opcache.file_cache_only=1 -d opcache.file_update_protection=0 test.php
```

Resulted in this output, on both runs:
```
Segmentation fault
```

But I expected this output instead:
```
array(1) {
  ["message"]=>
  string(3) "bar"
}
```

I reproduced it with the `i386/php:8.5-cli` Docker image. The same image gives the expected output without OPcache, and with the file cache for a constant without an attribute. `php:8.5-cli` on amd64 gives the expected output with the file cache.

The cause is in `zend_file_cache_serialize_op_array()` ([ext/opcache/zend_file_cache.c#L560-L565](https://github.com/php/php-src/blob/php-8.5.12/ext/opcache/zend_file_cache.c#L560-L565)):

```c
if (opline->opcode == ZEND_OP_DATA
    && (opline-1)->opcode == ZEND_DECLARE_ATTRIBUTED_CONST
) {
    zval *literal = RT_CONSTANT(opline, opline->op1);
    SERIALIZE_ATTRIBUTES(Z_PTR_P(literal));
}
```

`opline` points into the serialization buffer. With `ZEND_USE_ABS_CONST_ADDR` (32-bit builds), `RT_CONSTANT()` returns `opline->op1.zv`. That pointer is not serialized yet, so it still points to the literal in `script->mem`, not to its copy in `buf`. `SERIALIZE_ATTRIBUTES()` therefore rewrites the attributes pointer of the live script and leaves a raw pointer in the buffer:

- the current request loses the attributes of the constant;
- the `.bin` file stores an invalid pointer, which every later request loads.

On 64-bit builds, `RT_CONSTANT()` is relative to `opline`, so it already resolves into `buf`. `zend_file_cache_unserialize_op_array()` is correct, because it reads the literal after it unserializes `op1.zv`.

A possible fix, with the same pattern as the GH-17733 code for `ZEND_INIT_FCALL` a few lines below:

```c
zval *literal = RT_CONSTANT(opline, opline->op1);
#if ZEND_USE_ABS_CONST_ADDR
SERIALIZE_PTR(literal);
UNSERIALIZE_PTR(literal);
#endif
SERIALIZE_ATTRIBUTES(Z_PTR_P(literal));
```

### PHP Version

```plain
PHP 8.5.12 (cli) (built: Oct 21 2026 15:55:33) (NTS)
Copyright (c) The PHP Group
Built by https://github.com/docker-library/php
Zend Engine v4.5.12, Copyright (c) Zend Technologies
    with Zend OPcache v8.5.12, Copyright (c), by Zend Technologies
```

### Operating System

Debian, i386 (i386/php:8.5-cli Docker image under qemu on macOS arm64)

feat: Implement extension methods (RFC prototype, phase 1)
items.body:
Adds extension blocks that declare additional methods for an existing class or interface, resolved at call time only when the receiver's class does not define the method itself. Each block declares a named **receiver variable** — there is no `$this` in an extension body (C# 14 extension-member style):

```php
extension \DateTimeImmutable $date {
    public function isWeekend(): bool {
        return in_array((int)$date->format('N'), [6, 7], true);
    }
}

(new DateTimeImmutable('2026-07-11'))->isWeekend(); // true
```

### Mechanics

- `extension` is a contextual keyword (`T_EXTENSION`), lexed only when followed by another identifier, mirroring the `enum` technique; an `extension extends/implements` carve-out preserves classes named `extension`, and `T_EXTENSION` is semi-reserved. No BC break intended.
- Extension blocks compile to a synthetic final anonymous class; a new `ZEND_BIND_EXTENSION` opcode (212) registers its methods, keyed by the lowercased resolved target name, when the declaration executes (load-gated, like function declarations).
- `zend_std_get_method` gains one fallback on its miss path: real method → `__call` trampoline → extension registry lookup (most-derived target first: inheritance chain, then interfaces). A class's own methods of any visibility always shadow extensions.
- The receiver travels through the normal method calling convention (the frame's This slot) and is bound into the declared variable by a new `ZEND_RECV_RECEIVER` opcode (213), emitted after the parameter RECVs so the RECV-skip fast path lands on it. Because the body holds the receiver like any outside code holds an object reference, extension bodies see only the target's **public** API — the visibility rule falls out of the syntax.
- First-class callables of extension methods work: the closure binds the receiver at acquisition and `ZEND_RECV_RECEIVER` re-binds it on each invocation.

### Restrictions (all compile errors)

- `$this` anywhere in an extension body ("use the declared receiver").
- `static::` (no meaningful late-static-binding referent).
- Methods only: properties, constants, and cases are rejected (object layout is fixed at link time and shared under opcache).
- Magic methods (the reserved `__` prefix) — they dispatch through dedicated class-entry slots and handlers, never through the resolution path, so an extension-declared one could never behave as one. This also forecloses extensions injecting constructors.
- Reserved type names as targets (`extension string $s {}` is an error here; scalar targets are a separate, dependent proposal — see below).
- Abstract extension methods; a parameter shadowing the receiver; a receiver named `$this`.

### Opcache / JIT

The persisted class image is never mutated at runtime: everything the feature marks on the synthetic class (`ZEND_ACC_NEVER_CACHE` per method, bypassing the polymorphic inline cache) is applied at compile time and travels with the cached image; runtime registration only reads the persisted CE. The tracing JIT does not follow into never-cached bodies (same treatment as `__call` trampolines and property hooks). Verified green: full Zend + tokenizer suites, plain / `opcache.enable_cli=1 + opcache.protect_memory=1` / `opcache.jit=tracing` with run-tests' hotness settings, on NTS and ZTS debug builds.

### Known behavior under discussion

Paths resolving through `get_method` — `call_user_func([$obj,'m'])`, `is_callable`, `method_exists` (object form) — currently **do** see extensions; reflection does not. Whether to keep or restrict this is an open issue in the RFC.

### Prototype limitations

The registry is a process global: user-class method pointers dangle after request 1 in multi-request SAPIs (CLI-only until it moves into `zend_executor_globals`, which also needs to be preload-aware). Duplicate registrations are silently ignored (first wins); the final version should warn.

### Related

This is the base of a three-part proposal family, each with its own branch and (forthcoming) RFC:
- **Scalar extension methods** (`extension string $s { }`) — branch [`extension-methods-scalars`](https://github.com/hollyschilling/php-src/tree/extension-methods-scalars), stacked on this one.
- **Lexical visibility** (`extension Name on Target $t` + `use extension Vendor\Name;`) — branch [`extension-methods`](https://github.com/hollyschilling/php-src/tree/extension-methods), stacked on the scalars branch.

> Note for reviewers who saw earlier revisions: the receiver was originally bound to `$this`. That design was fully implemented and then rejected — semantically ($this implies inside-the-object access) and mechanically (extending it to non-object receivers required invasive frame-slot changes). The declared receiver variable reduced the engine footprint substantially; the RFC's Rejected Features section records the details.
